title: Plasma proteomics in epilepsy: network-based identification of proteins associated with seizures
projectDescription: Purpose Identification of potential biomarkers of seizures. Methods In this exploratory study, we quantified plasma protein intensities in 15 patients with recent seizures compared to 15 patients with long-standing seizure freedom. Using TMT-based proteomics we found fifty-one differentially expressed proteins. Results Network analyses including co-expression networks and protein-protein interaction networks, using the STRING database, followed by network centrality and modularity analyses revealed 22 protein modules, with one module showing a significant association with seizures. The protein-protein interaction network centered around this module identified a subnetwork of 125 proteins, grouped into four clusters. Notably, one cluster (mainly enriching inflammatory pathways and Gene Ontology terms) demonstrated the highest enrichment of known epilepsy-related genes.  Conclusion Overall, our network-based approach identified a protein module linked with seizures. The module contained known markers of epilepsy and inflammation. The results also demonstrate the potential of network analysis in discovering new biomarkers for improved epilepsy management.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Global relative quantitative proteomics Sample preparation Relative quantification was performed to compare plasma protein expression in epilepsy patients with and without seizures. High-abundance plasma proteins were removed using the High-Select™ Top14 abundant protein depletion resin kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) from 8µl of plasma following the manufacturer's incubation protocol. Flow-through was reduced (100mM DL-dithiothreitol, 60°C, 30 min) and processed using the modified filter-aided sample preparation (FASP) method (Wisniewski JR et. al. Nat Methods. 2009 May;6(5):359-62). In short, samples were concentrated and washed with 8M urea on Nanosep 30kDa  centrifugal filters ((Pall Corporation) and alkylated (MMTS, 10 mM, 30 min in room temperature). Samples were digested three sequential times for at least three hours with trypsin (0.3 µg, Pierce MS grade Trypsin, Thermo Fisher Scientific, 37°C) in digestion buffer (0.5 % sodium deoxycholate (SDC) 50 mM TEAB). A representative pool containing samples from both groups was used a references in the two TMT-sets. Peptides were isobaric labelled using Tandem Mass Tag (TMTpro, 18-plex) reagents (Thermo Fischer Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The labelled samples and the references were pooled into two TMT-sets, SDC was removed by acidification (10% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) and further purified using Pierce peptide desalting spin columns (Thermo Scientific), according to the manufacturer´s instructions.  The TMT-sets were fractionated by basic reversed-phase chromatography on a Dionex Ultimate 3000 UPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptide separations were performed using a reversed-phase XBridge BEH C18 column (3.5 μm, 3.5x150 mm, Waters Corporation) and a stepped gradient from 3% to 50% acetonitrile in 10 mM ammonium formate buffer (pH 10) over 30 min. 50 primary fractions were combined to 20 final fractions which were evaporated and reconstituted in 3% acetonitrile, 0.1% trifluoroacetic for LC-MS3 analysis.   Liquid chromatography coupled with tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS):  The fractions were analyzed on an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos Tribrid mass spectrometer with the FAIMS Pro ion mobility system, coupled with an Easy-nLC 1200 liquid chromatography system. Peptides were separated using reversed-phase chromatography with a gradient from 5.6% to 80% acetonitrile in 0.2% formic acid over 90 min at a flow of 300 nL/min. Double injections were performed with FAIMS Pro alternating between the compensation voltages (CV) of either -50/-75 or -40/-60, and the same data-dependent settings were used at all CVs. Precursor ion mass spectra were acquired at 120 000 resolution, scan range 375-1375 and maximum injection time 50 ms. MS2 analysis was performed in a data-dependent mode, where the most intense multiply charged precursors were isolated in the quadrupole with a 0.7 m/z isolation window and dynamic exclusion within 10 ppm for 60 s. The isolated precursors were fragmented by collision induced dissociation (CID) at 35% collision energy with the maximum injection time of 60 ms and detected in the ion trap, followed by multinotch (simultaneous) isolation of the top 12 MS2 fragment ions within the m/z range 400-1400, fragmentation (MS3) by higher-energy collision dissociation (HCD) at 55% collision energy and detection in the Orbitrap at 50 000 resolution m/z range 100-500 and maximum injection time 120 ms.
dataProcessingProtocol: Database matching and quantification Raw files were processed and analysed with Proteome Discoverer (ver 2.4, Thermo Fisher Scientific). The data was matched against Human SwissProt database (Jan 2022) using Mascot 2.5.1 (Matrix Science, London, United Kingdom)as a search engine with a precursor tolerance of 5 ppm and a fragment ion tolerance of 0.6 Da. Tryptic peptides were accepted with 0 missed cleavage. Methionine oxidation was set as a variable modifications and cysteine alkylation, TMTpro on lysine and peptide N-termini were set as fixed modifications. Percolator was used for PSM validation with a strict FDR threshold of 1%. For quantification TMT reporter ions were identified in the MS3 HCD spectra with 3 mmu mass tolerance and the TMT reporter intensity values for each sample were normalized on the total peptide amount. The SPS threshold was set to 65%. Only unique peptides were used for relative quantification and proteins were filtered at FDR of 5%.
